content: In the initial stages, pilot programs can be implemented, evaluated, and adjusted as necessary before scaling up. When designing an integrated approach to TB care for children and adolescents, several factors must be considered, including the existing health infrastructure (and the need for expansion or upgrades), regulatory frameworks, financing, operational research versus programmatic implementation, human resource requirements (such as staffing, capacity building, and training), monitoring and evaluation, and qualitative research into community needs, perceptions (including stigma), and suggestions. A differentiated service delivery (DSD) model, originally developed for HIV care, can be adapted for TB care. This person-centered approach simplifies and customizes services to meet the needs of individuals while optimizing health system resources. DSD principles can be applied to TB prevention, testing, linkage to care, treatment initiation, follow-up, and integration of TB care with co-infections and comorbidities. By offering families the choice to interact with the health system, DSD may facilitate the integration of child and adolescent TB services into primary healthcare or other programs. Examples of DSD implementation for children and adolescents at risk of or with TB are detailed in operational handbooks. Transitioning to decentralized, family-centered, and integrated TB services requires careful planning and regular monitoring of implementation. National TB programs (NTPs) must identify and address capacity needs for these interventions. Enhanced data collection on child and adolescent TB, while valuable, may require significant time and may only be feasible in specific operational research settings. Programs typically maintain registers for contact investigation, treatment registration, outcomes, and TB preventive treatment (TPT). These tools should be evaluated and improved through operational research. Monitoring should include the number of children diagnosed at various health system levels, the proportion with bacteriological confirmation, those clinically diagnosed, and those initiated and completing TPT. Data disaggregation by sex is important to assess gender equity impacts. Evaluating service quality across the patient pathway (screening, diagnosis, treatment) and client satisfaction is also essential. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides consolidated recommendations on TB care models for children and adolescents. These include health education and counseling on TB disease and treatment adherence, which can be supported by interventions such as SMS reminders, phone calls, medication monitors, and staff education. Interventions should be tailored to individual patient needs, provider resources, and implementation conditions. Suitable treatment administration options include video-supported treatment, communityor home-based treatment support, and support from trained lay providers or healthcare workers, which are preferred over unsupported or family-administered treatment. For multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), ambulatory care is recommended over hospitalization-based models, and decentralized care is preferred over centralized models. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all patients with presumptive or diagnosed TB. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for infants, children, and adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical or immune status, with priority given to children under five years old and those with advanced HIV disease. In high-prevalence settings for malaria or bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole should continue into adulthood, irrespective of antiretroviral therapy (ART) status. ART should be initiated for all individuals living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, with rapid initiation (within seven days of diagnosis) prioritized for those with advanced disease. For children and adolescents with TB, ART should begin within two weeks of starting TB treatment, except in cases of meningitis, where it should be delayed by at least four weeks. Nutritional care is critical for TB patients, particularly those with severe acute malnutrition. Children under five years old with TB and severe malnutrition should be managed according to WHO guidelines for severe acute malnutrition. For moderate undernutrition, school-age children, adolescents, and adults with TB who fail to regain normal body mass index after two months of treatment or lose weight during treatment should receive nutritional assessment, counseling, and locally available nutrient-rich or fortified foods. Nutritional screening should also be part of contact investigations for TB, with management aligned with WHO recommendations if malnutrition is identified. Research priorities include improving TB screening tools and approaches for children, evaluating integrated treatment decision algorithms, optimizing diagnostic methods (e.g., using stool samples or molecular diagnostics), and studying the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of shorter treatment regimens for drug-susceptible TB. For MDR-TB, research is needed on the safety, efficacy, and optimal use of drugs like bedaquiline and delamanid in children, as well as their cost-effectiveness and mechanisms of resistance. Additionally, studies on the management of TB meningitis, including shorter treatment regimens and their outcomes, are essential.
